audio_script: Electric charge is the source of the electric field. Place a positive charge at the origin, and the field points radially outward. Place a negative charge, and it points inward. This is the inverse-square law. The field falls off as one over r squared. On the right, you see the graph of that falloff. At distance one, the strength is one. At distance two, one quarter. At distance three, one ninth. That is why two charges twice as far apart feel one quarter the force. Now look at the arrow field on the left. Every arrow is the vector sum of contributions from every charge. This is the superposition principle. Here we have a dipole. A positive nanocoulomb at position minus one zero zero, and a negative nanocoulomb at position one zero zero. The field between them points from positive to negative. The magnitude at the midpoint is the sum of two contributions pointing the same way. That is four times what one charge alone would produce. Far away, the two charges nearly cancel, and the field dies off even faster, as one over r cubed. Numbers: with the Coulomb constant equal to nine times ten to the ninth, each charge produces a field of about nine newtons per coulomb at one meter. The visual arrows are normalized to the strongest field in the grid, but the underlying computation is exact Coulomb. The same inverse-square geometry that governs gravity governs electricity. Different charge, different constant, identical shape.

tagline: A twist you can read off two vectors

audio_script: The cross product of two vectors is a new vector. It points perpendicular to both, and its length is the product of their lengths times the sine of the angle between them. In two dimensions, the result is a scalar, the signed area of the parallelogram spanned by the two vectors. On the left, vector a is two comma zero point five. Vector b is negative zero point five comma one point five. Their cross product is two times one point five minus zero point five times negative zero point five, which is three point two five. That is also the area of the parallelogram on the right, computed from the same matrix. This is not a coincidence. Torque, which is r cross F, is the cross product of a position vector and a force. Its length is r times F times sine theta. If the force is parallel to the position vector, the cross product is zero. No torque. If the force is perpendicular, the torque is maximum. In three dimensions, the cross product is a vector whose direction follows the right-hand rule. But in two dimensions, we only need the scalar component perpendicular to the plane. On the left, the vectors. On the right, the parallelogram they span. Same number. That is what torque really is. It is the signed area of a certain parallelogram you can draw from the force and the lever arm.

tagline: Narrow pipe, faster fluid, lower pressure
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Bernoulli and the Venturi Effect", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 30}, {"type": "fluid_dynamics", "id": "flow", "operation": "venturi", "inlet_height": 1.8, "throat_height": 0.9, "length": 8.0, "inlet_velocity": 2.0, "density": 1000.0, "inlet_pressure": 101325.0, "particle_count": 16, "center": [0.0, -0.3, 0]}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "velocity up by 2x, pressure down by 15 kPa", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: Water flows through a pipe. Partway along, the pipe narrows to half its height. What happens to the water? Continuity says the volume entering must equal the volume exiting. Area times velocity is constant. So if the area halves, the velocity doubles. The water speeds up. From two meters per second at the inlet to four at the throat. Now Bernoulli's equation. The quantity pressure plus one half density times velocity squared is constant along a streamline. Since the velocity doubles at the throat, the kinetic energy term goes up by a factor of four. That rise has to come from somewhere, so the pressure drops. Plug in: inlet pressure is one atmosphere, one hundred one thousand three hundred twenty five pascals. Density is one thousand kilograms per cubic meter. At the throat, the pressure is lower by about fifteen thousand pascals. Notice that the fluid particles are visible in the animation. They crowd together at the throat because the cross section is narrower. Each particle speeds up and slows down as it traverses the pipe. This is exact: the particle velocity at any point equals inlet velocity times inlet height divided by local height. And the pressure is computed from Bernoulli directly, not sketched. This is why a carburetor works, and how a spray bottle atomizes liquid, and why a shower curtain pulls inward when you turn the shower on.

header_title: How a Curve Becomes a Series
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "How a Curve Becomes a Series", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 30}, {"type": "taylor_expand", "id": "series", "expr": "sin(x)", "x_range": [-3.0, 3.0], "max_terms": 6, "term_time": 1.3, "color": "#4CC9F0"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "each polynomial snaps closer to the curve", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: How do we compute a sine of any number? One answer, invented over centuries, is to replace the curve by a polynomial. Around zero, sine of x equals x minus x cubed over three factorial plus x to the fifth over five factorial, and so on forever. This is the Taylor series. The animation adds one term at a time. First, just x. A straight line through the origin. It matches sine only for tiny angles. Then minus x cubed over six. Now the curve bends down. Then plus x to the fifth over one twenty. It bends up again. Then minus x to the seventh over five thousand forty. The approximation now hugs the sine wave tightly between minus three and three. Each new term corrects the shape without changing the terms already drawn. This is why small-angle approximations work. For angles below about zero point three radians, the first term alone is accurate to one percent. For angles below one radian, the first two terms are enough. Beyond two radians, you need four or five terms. Every physics textbook that says sine theta is approximately theta is quietly using the first two terms of this series. Every calculator that computes sine uses about ten terms, plus a range reduction step. The series is not an approximation of sine. For analytic functions, the series is the function. The polynomial and the sine are the same object, written two different ways.

header_title: Resonance: When the Push Fits the Swing
tagline: Drive at the natural frequency, get the biggest response
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Resonance: When the Push Fits the Swing", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 28}, {"type": "driven_oscillator", "id": "drive", "anchor": [0.0, 2.0, 0], "rest_length": 1.8, "amplitude": 0.9, "period": 2.0, "color": "#4CC9F0"}, {"type": "calculus_graph", "id": "curve", "expression": "1/sqrt((x*x-1)**2 + 0.09)", "x_range": [0.0, 2.5], "y_range": [0.0, 4.0], "x_length": 3.2, "y_length": 2.6, "center": [5.5, 0.4, 0], "color": "#F1C40F"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "amplitude peaks when drive frequency equals natural", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: A mass on a spring. Give it a push at a certain frequency. If the push is slow, the mass just follows along gently. If the push is fast, the mass barely moves because the spring keeps reversing it. But if the push happens to match the natural frequency of the spring, the amplitude grows enormous. This is resonance. The equation of motion is mass times acceleration, plus damping times velocity, plus stiffness times displacement, equals the driving force. On the right, we plot the amplitude of the steady-state response against the drive frequency. The peak sits at the natural frequency, which is the square root of stiffness over mass. For this spring, natural frequency is one radian per second. On the left, the animation shows the mass being driven at exactly that frequency. Watch the amplitude grow. It would grow forever if there were no damping. The damping term limits the peak to a finite value. The sharpness of the peak is measured by a number called Q, which is the natural frequency divided by the damping rate. High Q means a narrow, tall peak. Low Q means a broad, short one. Push a child on a swing at the right rhythm, and the swing goes high. Push off rhythm, and it does not. Every radio receiver, every musical instrument, and every atom in a laser works on this principle.

tagline: A torque at right angles to the spin
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Gyroscope Precession", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 30}, {"type": "rotational_motion", "id": "rotor", "shape": "solid_disk", "mass": 1.5, "radius": 0.8, "angular_velocity": 6.0, "torque": 0.0, "center": [-3.5, 0.3, 0], "display_radius": 1.1, "color": "#4CC9F0"}, {"type": "angular_measurement", "id": "precession", "center": [3.5, 0.3, 0], "radius": 1.5, "start_angle": 0.0, "angle": 60.0, "color": "#F1C40F", "label": "Omega"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "spin fast, torque sideways, precess steadily", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: Spin a bicycle wheel rapidly. Hold the axle horizontal. Now try to tilt the axle downward. The wheel does not fall. It turns sideways. This is the gyroscope effect. The reason is angular momentum. The wheel has a large angular momentum along its axle, equal to its moment of inertia times its spin rate. When you apply a torque to change that direction, the change is perpendicular to both the torque and the angular momentum. So the axle does not go down. It goes around. The equation is torque equals the precession rate crossed with angular momentum. Solving for the precession rate gives torque divided by spin angular momentum. If the spin is fast, the precession is slow. If the spin is slow, the precession is fast. For our wheel: mass one point five, radius zero point eight, so moment of inertia equals one half times one point five times zero point six four, which is zero point four eight kilogram meters squared. Spin rate is six radians per second. Angular momentum is about two point eight eight. A small torque of zero point five newton meters gives a precession rate of zero point one seven four radians per second. On the left, the spinning disk. On the right, the precession cone it traces. The two panels are computed from the same numbers. Real gyroscopes maintain their orientation because this effect is precise and torque-resistant. This is why they were used in navigation before GPS.

visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "Fermat's Principle", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 34}, {"type": "geometry", "id": "path", "dimension": 2, "kind": "polyline", "points": [[-4.0, 1.5], [0.0, 0.0], [4.0, -1.0]], "color": "#4CC9F0", "stroke_width": 3}, {"type": "geometry", "id": "interface", "dimension": 2, "kind": "polyline", "points": [[-4.5, 0.0], [4.5, 0.0]], "color": "#8A8F9C", "stroke_width": 2}, {"type": "calculus_graph", "id": "time_curve", "expression": "sqrt((x+4)**2/4+2.25)+2*sqrt((4-x)**2+1)", "x_range": [-4.0, 4.0], "y_range": [3.0, 8.0], "x_length": 3.2, "y_length": 2.0, "center": [0.0, -5.0, 0], "color": "#F1C40F"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "refraction is the geometry of least time", "pos": [0.0, -7.5, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: Light travels from a point in air to a point in water. It does not go in a straight line. It bends at the surface. Why? Fermat's principle says: light takes the path that minimizes the total travel time. Not the shortest path. The fastest one. On the left, a path from A in air to B in water, crossing the interface at a point x. On the bottom, the total travel time as a function of x. The curve has a minimum. At that minimum, the path bends in exactly the way Snell's law predicts. The angle of incidence and the angle of refraction satisfy sine theta one over v one equals sine theta two over v two, where v one is the speed of light in air and v two is the speed in water. If we define the index of refraction as the ratio of speeds, this becomes Snell's law. This is why light bends toward the normal when entering a slower medium, and away from the normal when exiting. The animation shows the entire time curve. Every possible crossing point. The minimum is the actual path. This is one of the deepest principles in physics. It says that light does not just happen to follow Snell's law. It is the geometry of least time, and Snell's law is its derivative. The same principle governs mirror reflection, lens design, and even the trajectories of quantum particles in the limit of short wavelengths.

tagline: E and B perpendicular, in phase, transverse
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "The Electromagnetic Plane Wave", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 30}, {"type": "electromagnetic_wave", "id": "emwave", "amplitude": 1.0, "frequency": 0.8, "speed": 2.0, "length": 8.0, "phase": 0.0, "center": [0.0, 0.3, 0], "electric_color": "#4CC9F0", "magnetic_color": "#F1C40F"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "E perpendicular to B perpendicular to propagation", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: An electromagnetic wave. Two sinusoids travelling together, one for the electric field and one for the magnetic field. They are perpendicular to each other and both perpendicular to the direction of travel. This is a transverse wave. On screen, the top curve is the electric field. The bottom curve is the magnetic field. They oscillate in phase. When the electric field points up, the magnetic field points sideways, at right angles. Their ratio is a fixed number. The electric field divided by the magnetic field equals the speed of light. This relation is not assumed. It follows from Maxwell's equations. Light is not just electric. It is not just magnetic. It is the two fields locked together, each regenerating the other as they propagate. The direction of travel, the electric field, and the magnetic field form a right-handed triple. If you point your fingers along the electric field and curl them toward the magnetic field, your thumb points along the direction of travel. The speed is determined by two constants of the vacuum. The permittivity, which measures how strongly the vacuum responds to electric fields, and the permeability, which measures the same for magnetic fields. Take their product, take the square root, and you get the speed of light. That is why light propagates at three times ten to the eighth meters per second. It is a property of empty space, not of the source. This is the most extraordinary unification in physics.

tagline: Angular momentum does not care about shape
visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "The Spinning Skater", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 34}, {"type": "rotational_motion", "id": "arms_out", "shape": "solid_disk", "mass": 3.0, "radius": 1.4, "angular_velocity": 1.0, "torque": 0.0, "center": [-3.8, 0.3, 0], "display_radius": 1.3, "color": "#4CC9F0"}, {"type": "rotational_motion", "id": "arms_in", "shape": "solid_disk", "mass": 3.0, "radius": 0.7, "angular_velocity": 4.0, "torque": 0.0, "center": [3.8, 0.3, 0], "display_radius": 1.3, "color": "#F1C40F"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "inertia down by 4x, spin up by 4x, L constant", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: An ice skater spins. Arms out, slowly. Arms in, quickly. Nothing pushes her. No torque is applied. So her angular momentum must be conserved. Angular momentum equals moment of inertia times angular velocity. When she pulls her arms in, she reduces the moment of inertia. Since the product must stay constant, the angular velocity must increase by the same factor. On the left, arms out. Radius one point four. On the right, arms in. Radius zero point seven. The moment of inertia of a rotating body scales with radius squared, so halving the radius quarters the inertia. The angular velocity must then increase by a factor of four. On the left, spin rate is one radian per second. On the right, four. Watch the two spinners. They both have the same angular momentum, but they look completely different. This is not a special property of ice skates. It applies to neutron stars collapsing from the size of the sun to the size of a city, spinning up to hundreds of rotations per second. It applies to a child on a merry-go-round pulling in their legs. And it applies to an electron in an atom when its orbital state changes. Whenever a system is isolated and its moment of inertia decreases, its rotation speeds up. That is the conservation of angular momentum.

visual_data_json: [{"type": "text", "id": "title", "text": "The Potential Well", "pos": [0.0, 3.9, 0], "color": "#F2F3F5", "font_size": 34}, {"type": "potential_well", "id": "well", "width": 5.0, "height": 3.2, "n_state": 1, "pos": [-3.8, -0.3, 0], "color": "#4CC9F0", "wall_color": "#8A8F9C"}, {"type": "potential_well", "id": "well2", "width": 5.0, "height": 3.2, "n_state": 2, "pos": [3.8, -0.3, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "wall_color": "#8A8F9C"}, {"type": "text", "id": "caption", "text": "first two stationary states of an infinite well", "pos": [0.0, -4.15, 0], "color": "#F1C40F", "font_size": 16}]
audio_script: A particle confined to a box. It cannot leave. The walls are infinitely high. What are the possible energy states of this particle? In classical physics, any energy would do. In quantum mechanics, only certain discrete energies are allowed. The simplest case is the infinite square well. The wavefunction must vanish at the walls. Only sine waves fit that boundary condition. The lowest state, shown on the left, has half a wavelength across the box. The next state, on the right, has a full wavelength. Between the walls, there is a node where the wavefunction passes through zero. The energies are proportional to n squared, where n is the number of half-wavelengths that fit. The first energy is one unit. The second is four. The third is nine. When a particle drops from a higher state to a lower one, it emits a photon whose energy is the difference. For a box the size of an atom, the emitted light falls in the visible spectrum. For a box the size of a room, the spacing is far too small to detect. This is why quantum effects are invisible at human scales. The confinement is what quantizes the energy. Nothing else. Remove the walls, and the energies become continuous. Confine a wave, and it can only vibrate at certain frequencies.

For a solid cylinder about its central axis, inertia is one half mass times radius squared. Substitute: one half times four times zero point zero four. Zero point two squared is zero point zero four. Four times zero point zero four is zero point one six. Half of that is zero point zero eight. Option A. Compare this to a hollow cylinder with the same mass and radius.
